prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: a single part, B022, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. After the full first-round exchange the case rests on three things that I can check against what I know from the laboratory. First, the mechanism is a clean experimental idea: a magic-wavelength lattice cancels the differential light shift while removing Doppler and recoil broadening, so thousands of neutral atoms contribute to one measurement and the statistical limit moves by orders of magnitude relative to a single ion. Second, the outcome is a quantitative result that has been reproduced and compared across independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST), including the millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and the many-body, Fermi-degenerate clock regime. That is exactly the kind of demonstration I trust more than any proposal. Third, a new way of measuring is what opens fields, and here it has: relativistic geodesy, bounds on varying constants and on ultralight dark matter. On the chair's question about citation wording, I accept 'invention and realisation' for the concept and first demonstrations (Katori) and ask that the citation also name the 10^-18 performance (Ye and JILA), so that it answers both the members who want 'invention' and those who want 'development'. On the discovery-versus-tool objection, the demonstrated content to put in the case is the redshift across a millimetre and the many-body clock, which are measured effects and not prospective ones.
statement.case_against: The reservations that remain are real. This is a measurement advance whose largest scientific returns are still upper limits and consistency checks, and the committee has honoured the frequency comb (2005) and ion control (2012). Credit is also incomplete in the sense that Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Hollberg, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the comb and ion-clock groups shaped neighbouring steps, and I cannot establish priority from the packet beyond my own recollection. Ye's share is partly the work of a large JILA team, as the chair notes. The redefinition of the second has not happened. I judge none of these decisive, but I would not call the credit above criticism and I do not want to pretend otherwise.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube (B002) to B022 and, while still carrying field closeness to B002, did not defend it as ready this year; he also notes that Ye's share is partly the work of a large JILA team.
responses.response: I agree with your move, and with your own reasons for it: a single credited name for IceCube and its AMANDA predecessor cannot be defended on this pack, and TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 are still at modest significance. On your JILA point, I accept that the record performance is a team result, but the rules limit us to named people, and the decisive systematic-control programme at 10^-18 was led by Ye. I would therefore keep two names and say so in the citation by crediting the invention and the realisation, and not claim that two people did everything.

responses.point: Lindroth resists widening the credit beyond Katori and Ye, asks how to weigh Katori's concept against the JILA record performance, and keeps B020 only as an alternative because Greiner's experiment is not settled in any three-name set.
responses.response: I agree that we should not widen the credit, and I would support her on that against any request to add Lemonde or Gill without primary evidence, which none of us has in the packet. On the weighting, I think the two-clause citation answers it: Katori for the lattice idea and first demonstrations, Ye for the realisation at 10^-18. On B020 I now share her view that the three-name set is the obstacle (Greiner, Bloch, Zoller, with Esslinger and Cirac left out), and because of that I do not propose a second part from it. A second part would also weaken the cleanest attribution on the list.

responses.point: Olsson ranked B038 first at opening, moved to B022, and keeps a worry that clocks are a tool awaiting the redefinition of the second, while judging the scientific maturity sufficient.
responses.response: I agree with your final judgement and I would answer the redefinition worry directly: the SI decision follows from agreement between independent clocks at the 10^-18 level, and does not validate it. If the committee waited for the CGPM, it would be waiting for a metrological convention and not for a missing scientific demonstration. I also respect your original case for B038: room-temperature TMR is a clear, reproducible experimental effect. I leave it out of my configuration because of the credit gap for the MgO result (Yuasa and others) and the overlap with the 2007 GMR prize.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from B018 to B022 but concedes it is an instrument and measurement achievement and not a new state of matter, and fears it reads as the same territory as 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I take the discovery-versus-instrument point seriously because I weigh measurement heavily and so I ought to be the one to say what is different. The 2005 prize covered the comb as a tool and 2012 covered control of single quantum systems; neither covers many-atom interrogation in a lattice, which is what changes the statistical limit and is what gives the many-body clock physics. If the citation is written around the lattice concept and the 10^-18 performance, and not around timekeeping in general, as you propose, I think that separation is visible to any reader.

responses.point: Johansson asks the committee to keep the citation on demonstrated precision and the redshift measurement and not on prospective dark-matter and constants searches, and keeps B020 and B043 as alternatives.
responses.response: I agree and I have changed my own wording to follow it: the citation should rest on the demonstrated 10^-18 precision, and the case text can mention the redshift and many-body results as measured effects. I would treat dark matter and varying constants as the reason the field matters, not as a claim of discovery. On alternatives I differ slightly from you: I keep B004 and B043 over B020, because a quantum-simulation set cannot be reduced to three names without an arbitrary exclusion.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will read optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes once the citation names the lattice and the 10^-18 performance.
Whether Katori and Ye are an adequate credit set against Lemonde, Hollberg, Gill and others, which I cannot verify beyond recollection.
Whether the committee wishes to wait for the redefinition of the second; I think not, but members who value a societal endorsement may disagree.
Whether B004 or B043 could ever be given a clean credited set if B022 does not carry: Chu is not in the supplied B004 names and B043 has its own priority questions.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. During my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye is a long-standing close collaborator of Hall at JILA. I have no direct collaboration, supervision or institutional tie to Katori or Ye, and the stay was decades ago. I state this as a mild personal link to the B022 community and leave it to the chair and the committee to decide whether any step beyond disclosure is needed; I do not think so, and I will accept the committee's decision. Separately, I am in the leadership of WACQT (Chalmers-led) and would recuse from any decision that depends on B014 (circuit QED), as Johansson also states for himself. My own field of rare-earth-ion quantum memories and slow light gives no tie to B004 or B043.
